summary.value: This paper proposes MoVie, a multimodal learned video compression framework that introduces textual guidance to improve perceptual quality at low complexity. Reviewers found the paper to be clearly written and technically sound, and acknowledged the efficiency of the proposed architecture. However, the main concerns lie in the overall strength of the contribution. In particular, the experimental evaluation does not provide sufficiently comprehensive comparisons with recent perception-oriented video compression methods, the effectiveness of the proposed approach appears to be highly sensitive to the quality of the textual guidance and thus lacks robustness, and some key architectural choices remain weakly justified. Despite improvements made in the rebuttal, these issues collectively limit the impact of the work and lead to a recommendation for rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value: Concerns regarding missing or insufficient comparison with perception-oriented baselines were partially addressed by the rebuttal, but the evaluation remains incomplete. Issues related to the sensitivity of the method to textual guidance quality were partially addressed, but the stability and generality of the gains remain unclear. Concerns about the motivation and justification of the architectural design, especially the text integration mechanism, are still outstanding.

reviewer_scores.value: The paper initially received one borderline accept, three borderline rejects, and one reject. Based on the rebuttal, the reviewer who gave the borderline accept (ytLC) expressed openness to revising their evaluation. For the remaining reviewers, it is likely that their core concerns are not fully resolved, and their assessments are therefore expected to remain unchanged.

comment.value:
> Unclear motivation for Text-VideoTCM design. As a core contribution, the design rationale of the Text-VideoTCM module is underexplained. The idea of using two successive stages for extraction and injection is presented as an architectural choice but lacks clear theoretical or empirical justification. It is not evident why this two-step process is superior to a simpler single-stage cross-attention mechanism. The current explanation appears heuristic rather than principle-driven.

Thank you for pointing this out — we agree that the design rationale of Text-VideoTCM needed to be explained more clearly, especially in contrast to simpler single-stage cross-attention.

From image-level to video-level text guidance.  
Prior text-guided image compression works such as TACO operate in a one-to-one setting: each image has its own caption, and a single-stage cross-attention between image tokens and text tokens is indeed a natural and effective choice. In our video setting, however, we typically have one clip-level description for a sequence of frames, and fine-grained per-frame captions are not available. Directly reusing the image-style design (one global caption, single-stage fusion with every frame) ignores that different frames may only partially match the global text and often contain additional, frame-specific content.

Why a simple single-stage cross-attention is insufficient.  
We tested exactly this “simpler” design: using the global clip caption and fusing it directly with each frame’s visual tokens in a single cross-attention stage. These configurations correspond to the revised Table 3, where the same text embedding is injected into every frame without our two-stage alignment. Empirically, these variants give noticeably worse perceptual reconstruction quality than our proposed Text-VideoTCM, confirming that naïvely broadcasting a global caption to all frames is not an effective way to exploit text in video.

Rationale of the two-stage Text-VideoTCM.
Our two-stage scheme is designed precisely to adapt a single clip-level caption to a sequence of frames:

Stage 1 (Extraction): We use the global sentence embedding together with each frame’s visual tokens to derive frame-specific text features. Intuitively, this step answers “which parts of the caption are actually relevant to this frame?”, producing pseudo per-frame textual guidance rather than reusing the same global token everywhere.

Stage 2 (Injection): These frame-specific text features are then fed into the Video Swin–Transformer backbone (VideoTCM) and fused temporally, so that the model can propagate both visual and aligned textual cues along the time axis in a causal manner.

Conceptually, this separates cross-modal alignment (text–frame matching in Stage 1) from spatio–temporal modeling (VideoTCM in Stage 2), which we found to be more appropriate for the “one caption + many frames” structure of video.

Empirical justification (Table 3).
In the revised manuscript, we explicitly report the single-stage variants in Table 3 and compare them with our two-stage Text-VideoTCM. Under the same autoencoder training setting, the two-stage design consistently achieves better perceptual reconstruction metrics than the single-stage cross-attention baselines, indicating that the additional “extraction then injection” structure is not merely heuristic, but provides a practical benefit in the video regime.

| Copy Text                   | 230.76      | 190ms          | 44.59  | 0.99789   | 0.0212        | 0.0020        |
| **Two-stage Text(MoVie)**  | 235.12      | 197ms          | **46.49**  | **0.99796**   | **0.0041**    | **0.0009**    |
Thanks for rebuttal! All concerns are addressed, and I decide to accept this paper.

> Limited novelty beyond prior multimodal compression works. While MoVie emphasizes the use of textual priors, this idea was first introduced in TACO for text-guided image compression. MoVie does not clearly extend this concept to address video-specific challenges such as temporal semantic consistency or cross-frame alignment. Consequently, its multimodal contribution seems incremental rather than substantially innovative.

Thank you for your careful assessment of the novelty and for explicitly connecting our work to prior multimodal compression methods such as TACO. We fully agree that our work builds on important prior lines of research, including text-guided image compression (e.g., TACO [1]) and Transformer–CNN hybrids [2], and we have revised the paper to state this more clearly. At the same time, we would like to clarify that MoVie is not a direct transplant of TACO to video nor a generic reuse of existing hybrid architectures; rather, it introduces several video-specific and text-specific design choices that explicitly target temporal semantic consistency and cross-frame alignment:

From text-guided images to text-guided video compression.
Prior text-conditioned codecs such as TACO operate on single images and do not consider temporal prediction, causality, or inter-frame dependencies. To the best of our knowledge, MoVie is among the first attempts to extend text guidance to learned video compression, where (i) text must be integrated into a temporal prior, (ii) the model must respect causal decoding, and (iii) the effect of text must propagate consistently across many frames. This change in problem setting fundamentally affects how guidance is injected and how the latent prior is modeled over time.

Video-specific Swin–CNN hybrid (VideoTCM) with text injection.
Instead of reusing the image-level TCM from [1], we design a Video Swin Transformer–3D CNN hybrid (VideoTCM) that explicitly models spatio–temporal structure. Text is injected into this video backbone in a way that (a) aligns with Swin’s local windowing for spatial locality, and (b) propagates along the temporal axis through VideoTCM, so that the same semantic cue can maintain cross-frame alignment in a causal sequence. We also ablate text usage on the encoder-side prior and decoder-side reconstruction paths (Sec. 3 / Table 3), going beyond the encoder-only conditioning typical of TACO-style image codecs.

Spatial–channel entropy model extended with a temporal cache.
While spatial–channel factorization itself is known, our entropy model combines (i) window-based $8\times 8$ spatial partitioning, (ii) sequential channel-slice modeling within each window, and (iii) a temporal cache of historical latents fused by VideoTCM to form the prior for each frame (Sec. 3.3). This yields a unified design that jointly exploits spatial locality, channel factorization, and long-range temporal dependencies in the latent space, which is not present in [1,2] or in standard spatial–channel models.

Two-stage, video-adaptive text guidance for temporal consistency.
We propose a two-stage text conditioning scheme tailored to video: in the first stage, we obtain per-frame text features aligned with each frame; in the second stage, these frame-level textual features are fused temporally via VideoTCM to produce a global yet time-aware guidance signal. This is different from image codecs that only use a single, static global text embedding and therefore do not address how text interacts with temporal dynamics or semantic consistency across frames. Our ablations (Table 3) show that this two-stage scheme works better than simpler single-stage text fusion when only a clip-level caption is available.

We have revised the introduction and related work sections to better position our contributions relative to TACO [1], Transformer–CNN hybrids [2], and multimodal/spatial–channel compression models, and we have softened overly broad claims. Our goal is not to claim that each building block is entirely new in isolation, but to show that bringing text guidance into a causal, perceptual learned video codec requires non-trivial, video-specific adaptations in both the backbone and the entropy model, and that MoVie designs, analyzes, and ablates these adaptations with explicit attention to temporal semantic consistency and cross-frame alignment.

> Minor technical issue. In Figure 2, the notation “x” is overloaded — it denotes both the input/output in the left figure and the representaions after fusion conv in the right part.

Thank you for pointing this out. In the revised version, we keep using $x$ to denote the input/output frames in the left part of Fig. 2, but we have renamed the representations after the fusion conv in the right part from $x$ to $m$. The figure and the corresponding description are updated accordingly, so that each symbol now has a unique and unambiguous meaning.

summary.value: This paper proposes a framework called MoVie, a perception-oriented video compression method. MoVie introduces textual information at the encoder to enhance perceptual compression quality. Compared to previous objectively oriented compression methods, it achieves a significant improvement in perceptual quality while also substantially reducing complexity.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed method achieves a significant improvement in perceptual quality compared to previous approaches.
2. The proposed method achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity.
3. The design of the text information introduction module and the entropy model has some innovations.
4. This paper is easy to understand.

weaknesses.value:
1. The necessity of introducing text information is not adequately verified.
2. The methods used in the comparisons are all objective compression methods, which cannot determine whether the improvement in perception quality is due to excellent model design or simply the introduction of a loss function related to perception quality.

questions.value:
1. The necessity of introducing text still requires further validation. For example, keeping the complexity identical during training but replacing the text input with a constant, and then training another set of models, would provide more convincing evidence. The paper only presents comparisons with different text inputs after training is completed, as well as comparisons where complexity is not kept consistent (I understand that the complexity of "+VideoTCM+S-C" and "+VideoTCM+S-C-Text" should be different, due to the "Extractor" and "Injector"?). Therefore, I still have doubts about the actual contribution of the textual information to the final perceptual quality.
2. I can understand introducing textual information at the decoder side, as in compression scenarios the decoder can be viewed as video generation, and using text for a generation task is quite natural. However, due to causality considerations, the authors only introduce textual information at the encoder side. Since the encoder's typical role is de-correlation, I am uncertain whether the textual information truly contributes to this process. Does the encoder in perception-oriented video compression have functions beyond de-correlation? Could the authors further explain the rationale for introducing textual information at the encoder side, beyond just causality concerns?
3. Are there any other perception-oriented video compression methods available for comparison? For example, “Generative Latent Coding for Ultra-Low Bitrate Image and Video Compression”?

> Questions: Why was the image-based Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) used to evaluate video perceptual quality instead of the more standard and appropriate Fréchet Video Distance (FVD), which is designed to assess temporal consistency?

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) is a more appropriate metric than image-based FID for assessing temporal consistency in video. In the revised manuscript, we therefore add FVD as an additional evaluation metric and report it for all compared methods in a new table. As shown there, MoVie achieves consistently better or comparable FVD scores than the baselines, indicating that the perceptual gains observed in FID also hold when measuring temporal coherence.
We retain FID mainly for continuity with prior learned video compression works that still report image-based perceptual metrics, but now explicitly complement it with FVD to more faithfully reflect video-level perceptual quality.

summary.value: This paper introduces a text-guided learned video compression scheme (termed MoVie). Like VCT, MoVie skips low-level motion estimation and motion compensation, in the hopes of preserving perceptual quality in complex scenes. To this end, the proposed feature extractor incorporates 3D window-based Transformer and 3D CNN to create a video-focused latent generator (i.e. encoder). This is distinct from the image-based feature extractor adopted by VCT. Moreover, to enhance semantic preservation, the proposed feature extractor adopts a dual-stage text fusion mechanism. Reportedly, it outperforms the SOTA DCVC codecs in terms of FID and LPIPS. Furthermore, it requires only half of the kMAC/pixels of DCVC-FM.

strengths.value:
The performance results look interesting. 
The dual-stage text fusion mechanism appears novel. 
The low kMAC/pixel is another striking point of this work. 
This is one of the few early attempts at textual-guided video compression for perceptual quality optimization.

weaknesses.value:
1. The comparison with the DCVC series is unfair in that they are not really optimized for perceptual quality. Neither does VCT. I understand that there are only few perceptually optimized learned video codecs, the code of which may not be available. For a fair comparison, it would be instructive to see how MoVie compares with the DCVC series of work if its training objective involves only MSE or MS-SSIM as the only distortion metric. That is, I would like to see the performance of MSE-optimized MoVie and MS-SSIM-optimized MoVie for a fair comparison with the other baselines, given that it is nearly impossible to re-train these codecs for perceptual quality. 
2. Line 202: While I understand that the textual description is a form of global information, it does not make much sense to me that such global information is only used on the encoder side but not on the decoder side. The argument that injecting it into entropy coding or decoding would break frame-wise causality is NOT very convincing. The textual information can be signaled in the bitstream with a minimal impact on the compressed bit-rate. Since it can be easily made available on both sides as causal contextual information, why not use it? It would be instructive to see the performance of the following 4 variants: Encoder (Text-VideoTCM vs. VideoTCM) + Decoder (Text-VideoTCM vs. VideoTCM). 
3. Please report encoding and decoding times as the block-wise spatial AR modeling is involved. Note that VCT allows multiple blocks to be decoded simultaneously. This does not seem possible with the spatial AR modeling.  
4. Like VCT, the proposed method does NOT perform explicit motion estimation and compensation. It would be instructive to see how the proposed method works on those fast- or complex-motion sequences. In addition, to compensate for motion, VCT has an extended search window in the latent space (y space). With VideoTCM (the left part of Fig. 3) for fusing y_{i-1} and y_{<i}, it appears that there is no notion of extended window. This design reinforces my impression that motion compensation is done implicitly via VideoTCM.

questions.value:
Line 247: I suppose that the textual description is a sentence composed of a sequence of words. However, it appears that only ONE global textual token of 512 dimensions serves as the query to aggregate information from visual tokens extracted from each video frame. Why only ONE token? Or there are actually multiple textual tokens. If this is the case, the description needs updating. In addition, to my surprise, only one linear layer is sufficient to project visual tokens into the textual space of CLIP and vice versa. 
In Fig. 2, it is unclear whether only one textural description is used for the entire test sequence (of 96 frames long or even longer). 
Please clarify how many frames are processed together as a whole. How does the proposed method impact the coding delay? Most learned codecs process video on a frame-by-frame basis for both feature extraction and coding. They could support low-delay or random-access applications depending on the temporal prediction structure. But, with the proposed scheme, this part becomes unclear.

The argument that injecting it into entropy coding or decoding would break frame-wise causality is NOT very convincing. Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We agree that, in principle, the textual description can be signaled in the bitstream at negligible rate and thus made available on the decoder side as causal context. In the original submission we used text only on the encoder-side prior network (Text-VideoTCM in the entropy model) and kept the decoder VideoTCM text-free, mainly to keep the architecture close to the video-only baseline and to isolate the effect of text on the learned prior.

Following your suggestion, the revised Table 2 now reports all four variants you proposed:
| Method                    | kMACs/pixel | Inference time | PSNR       | MS-SSIM       | FID           | LPIPS   |
|-------------------------  |------------:|---------------:|--------:   |----------:    |--------:      |--------:|
| Enc-V / Dec-V (Vie)       | **226.07**  | **187ms**      | **46.78**  | **0.99826**   | 0.0062        | 0.0018  |
| **Enc-T / Dec-V (MoVie)** | 235.12      | 197ms          | 46.49      | 0.99796       | **0.0041**    | **0.0009**|
| Enc-V / Dec-T             | 235.12      | 196ms          | 45.08      | 0.99673       | 0.0053        | 0.0012  |
| Enc-T / Dec-T             | 244.11      | 206ms          | 45.69      | 0.99686       | 0.0057        | 0.0012  |

The autoencoder experiments show that (i) introducing text at the encoder side (Text-VideoTCM encoder) brings the dominant perceptual gain at comparable bitrates, and (ii) adding text also at the decoder side yields only modest additional improvements over MoVie, while text only at the decoder (VideoTCM encoder + Text-VideoTCM decoder) is noticeably less effective. 

A plausible explanation is that, during autoencoder training, the encoder determines what information is preserved in the latent space. When text is injected at the encoder side, the latent representation is shaped to align with semantic cues, so the decoder can reconstruct text-relevant structures more faithfully from a coherent latent. If text is introduced only at the decoder, the latent remains video-only and the decoder must “correct” or hallucinate details from insufficient features, which can conflict with the latent and degrade both fidelity and perceptual quality. Injecting text on both sides over-conditions the model with similar guidance twice, making optimization harder without providing additional semantic information beyond the encoder-side guidance, which explains why Enc-T/Dec-T does not outperform the simpler Enc-T/Dec-V design.




> Please report encoding and decoding times as the block-wise spatial AR modeling is involved. Note that VCT allows multiple blocks to be decoded simultaneously. This does not seem possible with the spatial AR modeling.

Thank you for pointing this out. In the revised manuscript, Table 2 now reports average per-frame encoding and decoding wall-clock times, as well as the separate computational complexity of the encoder and decoder (kMACs) for MoVie and all baselines. This directly quantifies the overhead introduced by our block-wise spatial AR entropy model compared to non-AR baselines such as VCT.

In addition, we have expanded Sec. 3.3 to clarify how our AR modeling operates: it is performed within non-overlapping $8\times 8$ spatial windows and along channel slices, so different windows (and different frames in a batch) can still be processed in parallel, while the autoregressive dependency is restricted to slices within a window. We hope these additions address your concern about practical decodability and make the trade-off between our spatial AR design and VCT’s more parallel decoding strategy more transparent.

The framework employs a dual-stage text fusion mechanism to integrate semantic priors. **Limited Novelty**

The central idea of incorporating text guidance in the encoder is largely derived from prior work in image compression, particularly TACO [1], without introducing substantial modifications for video compression. The spatial–channel entropy model is also well established in the video codec research domain.

The paper positions itself as a strong perceptual compression model, yet it does not compare against other specialized baselines designed explicitly for perceptual quality. The comparison is limited to standard SOTA codecs (VCT, DCVC) rather than dedicated perceptual models [3,4,5]. This omission makes the claim of state-of-the-art perceptual quality less robust. Since the captions are generated by large language models (LLMs), the computational complexity of these models should also be taken into account in the overall encoding process.

summary.value: The paper introduces MoVie, a multimodal video compression framework that integrates textual guidance into a spatiotemporally-aware deep autoencoder. The core contribution is a Text-guided Video Transformer-CNN Mixed block (Text-VideoTCM) that fuse CLIP-derived textual semantics with localized spatiotemporal dependencies using a dual-branch Video Swin Transformer and 3D CNN architecture. MoVie also proposes a history-conditioned, spatial-channel factorized entropy model to better capture temporal and channel dependencies for improved rate control and perceptual quality. Extensive experiments on UVG, MCL-JCV, and HEVC datasets show substantial BD-rate reductions (notably on perceptual metrics) and compute efficiency compared to strong learned and traditional baselines.

strengths.value:
**1) Compelling integration of multimodal guidance:**  MoVie leverages CLIP text features through a well-motivated two-stage fusion (Extractor and Injector), improving semantic coherence in reconstructions.

**2) Innovation in architecture:** The mixed Video Swin Transformer and 3D CNN block (Text-VideoTCM) cleverly balances localized detail and high-level semantics.

**3) Sound entropy modeling:** The proposed spatial-channel factorized entropy model conditions on both prior and historical frames, which is well justified for videos.

**1) Limited theoretical transparency in entropy model:** Although the spatial-channel factorized entropy model is formally described (Figure 3, Section 3.3), the concrete mathematical instantiation, especially how channel groupings interact with window-based spatial splits and how sequential channel entropy coding unrolls over temporally cached states, is not fully specified. Dear reviewer S5kW,

We would like to thank you for the very detailed review and the constructive feedback you provided! Below, we address your concerns in detail:
> Limited Novelty

Thank you for your careful assessment of the novelty. We fully agree that our work builds on important prior lines of research, including text-guided image compression (e.g., TACO [1]) and Transformer–CNN hybrids [2], and we have revised the paper to state this more explicitly. At the same time, we would like to clarify that our method is not a direct transplant of TACO to video nor a generic reuse of existing hybrid architectures; rather, it introduces several video-specific and text-specific design choices:

Problem setting: from text-guided images to text-guided video compression.  
Prior text-conditioned codecs such as TACO operate on single images and do not consider temporal prediction, causality, or inter-frame dependencies. To the best of our knowledge, MoVie is among the first attempts to extend text guidance to learned video compression, where (i) text must be integrated into a temporal prior, (ii) the model must respect causal decoding, and (iii) the effect of text must propagate consistently across many frames. This change in problem setting significantly affects how the guidance is injected and how the entropy model is formulated.

Video-specific Swin–CNN hybrid with text injection.  
Instead of reusing the image-level TCM from [1], we design a Video Swin Transformer–3D CNN hybrid (VideoTCM) that explicitly models spatio–temporal structure. Text is injected into this video backbone in a way that propagates across time through VideoTCM, rather than only modulating single-frame features.

Spatial–channel entropy model extended with temporal cache.  
While spatial–channel factorization is indeed known, our entropy model combines (i) window-based $8\times 8$ spatial partitioning, (ii) sequential channel-slice modeling within each window, and (iii) a temporal cache of historical latents fused by VideoTCM to form the prior for each frame (Sec. 3.3). This yields a unified design that jointly exploits spatial locality, channel factorization, and long-range temporal dependencies in the latent space, which is not present in [1,2] or in standard spatial–channel models.

Two-stage, video-adaptive text guidance.  
We propose a two-stage text conditioning scheme tailored to video: in the first stage, we obtain per-frame text features aligned with each frame; in the second stage, these frame-level textual features are fused temporally via VideoTCM to produce a global yet time-aware guidance signal. This is different from image codecs that only use a single, static global text embedding and do not need to consider how text interacts with temporal dynamics or coding delay.

We have revised the introduction and related work sections to better position our contributions relative to TACO [1], Transformer–CNN hybrids [2], and spatial–channel entropy models, and we have toned down overly broad claims. Our goal is not to claim that each building block is conceptually new in isolation, but to show that bringing text guidance into a causal, learned video codec requires non-trivial architectural and entropy-model adaptations, which we design, analyze, and ablate in detail.

temporal modeling.

remarkable reduction in per-pixel MACs (only 55.76% of DCVC-FM) while maintaining
competitive perceptual performance. This shows that the hybrid VideoTCM design is efficient

Thank you for pointing out these ambiguities — we agree that the original description around Line 247 was not sufficiently precise, and we have clarified it in the revision.

How many text tokens / what dimension?  
In our implementation, we do not use a single 512-dimensional global text token. Instead, the textual description is first tokenized by the CLIP tokenizer, and then encoded by a frozen CLIP text encoder into a sequence of tokens. We have revised the description in the paper to "The textual description is encoded by a frozen CLIP text encoder into $t \in \mathbb{R}^{L\times512}\$, where we fix the token length to $L=38$ by truncating or padding the CLIP token sequence."

Why “one global token” vs multiple tokens?  
For the global conditioning path (e.g., the global text token shown in Fig. 2), we pool the CLIP sequence into a single sentence embedding and use it as a lightweight global modifier to the video prior. However, in the two-stage Text-VideoTCM design, we also use the full sequence of text tokens in the Extractor stage to derive frame-specific text features before injecting them into the VideoTCM backbone. The revised text now explicitly distinguishes between the pooled global sentence embedding and the sequence-level features used for per-frame alignment.

How many frames per text and impact on delay?  
Following common practice, we use clips of 96 frames for evaluation. Due to GPU memory limits, during inference we process them with an effective batch size of 8 frames, i.e., each 8-frame chunk shares one textual description (one caption per 8-frame segment). Importantly, although features are computed in 8-frame chunks, the coding itself is strictly causal: for frame $i$, the entropy prior depends only on previously decoded latents $\hat{y}_{<i}$ via VideoTCM, and never on future frames. > Complexity issues

Thank you for raising this point. In our work, we treat the textual captions as side information that is available at encoding time (e.g., user-provided descriptions, editorial metadata, or captions pre-computed once by a separate captioning/VLM system), and we focus our complexity analysis on the video codec itself (encoder, decoder, and entropy model). This is consistent with prior text-guided compression and generation works, where the cost of obtaining text is not included in the codec’s compute budget. In many practical scenarios (video platforms, surveillance with structured logs, human-curated datasets), text–video pairs naturally exist or captions are generated offline and reused multiple times, so the LLM/VLM cost is amortized and decoupled from per-encode complexity. In the revised manuscript, we explicitly clarify this assumption in the experimental/complexity section and state that our reported MACs and runtimes exclude caption generation, which we regard as an auxiliary pre-processing step rather than part of the core video compression pipeline.

> Questions: Could the authors provide a specific breakdown of the decoder's complexity (kMACs or actual FPS/latency)? The proposed spatial-channel factorized entropy model appears to have sequential dependencies (Section 3.3) that could create a decoding bottleneck, which is not captured by the reported autoencoder-only MACs.

Thank you for pointing this out. In the revised manuscript, we now provide a more detailed decoder-side complexity analysis. Specifically, Table 1 has been updated to report separate encoding and decoding kMACs, as well as average decoding FPS / latency per frame, so that the cost of the full codec (including entropy decoding) is explicitly quantified rather than inferred only from the autoencoder MACs.

In addition, we have expanded Sec. 3.3 to clarify how the spatial–channel factorized entropy model is implemented in practice: the autoregressive dependency is restricted to channel slices within each non-overlapping 
$8 \times 8$ spatial window, while different windows (and different frames in a batch) can still be processed in parallel. This makes the scope of sequential operations and their impact on decoding throughput more transparent, and we hope the new measurements and description address your concern about a potential decoding bottleneck.
